source_read: Journal pre-proof PDF (Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews, accepted 23 September 2019): an unnumbered cover page, then manuscript pages printed 1-72 (PDF page = printed page + 1); anchors cite 'p. N of the journal pre-proof'. All text, the reference list and Table 1 (pp. 65-72) read. Text extracted with pdftotext -layout into my own folder (watermark letters stripped in a working copy); numbers checked on rendered pages (text pp. 12-13, 15, 17, 19-23 and 33 at 100 dpi; Table 1, pp. 65-72, at 150 dpi). Appendices A-H not in the file and not read. Only the parts of cl_can_cbd_with_thc that come from Freeman et al. (2019) were checked; the Zamarripa et al. (2023) part is another source.

claims.overstatement: (1) 'mostly occasionally' is not shown by the review. The text says only that all but two studies required previous cannabis use (p. 15); Table 1 shows frequency was mixed and often unreported: about half of Bird et al.'s 155 used at least weekly (p. 66), 24 of the 48 in the Hindocha/Morgan study used daily (p. 68), Haney et al.'s 31 are described as current users (p. 68), and Englund, Guy and Robson, Hollister and Gillespie and the users in Karniol are described only as having used at least once (pp. 67, 69). 'Almost all' is right: 18 of Karniol's 40 and 3 of Zuardi's 8 had never used cannabis, 21 of 466 (editors' arithmetic). (2) 'shortly before' understates the pre-treatment gaps: oral CBD was given 90 to 480 minutes before THC (p. 15; Table 1: 90 min Haney, 210 min Englund, 480, 300 and 120 min Hunt), CBD 30 minutes before in one Dalton experiment and intravenous CBD about 5 minutes before (Bhattacharyya). Everything else this claim takes from Freeman et al. is supported, and the claim correctly reports, rather than adopts, the discussion's statement that three studies showed significantly fewer people with extreme effects.
claims.note: Checked on the rendered pages: search on 28 February 2019 (pp. 10, 12); 16 studies in 23 articles, 1974 (Karniol) to 2019 (Arkell; Hindocha 2019; Wall 2019); 3 parallel-group (Bird, Englund, Karniol) and 13 crossover with Dalton's two experiments counted separately as in Table 1; n 4 to 155, total 466, which I reproduce from Table 1 with Bird 155, Dalton 16 + 8, Nadulski 24 and Arkell 14; all healthy volunteers (p. 15); narrative synthesis only (p. 17). Pharmacokinetics: eight studies, mostly no significant change; Arkell (n = 14) higher peak, AUC higher but not significantly; Guy and Robson (n = 24) later tmax (pp. 17-18). The discussion (pp. 32, 36) counts Nadulski et al. (2005) as a second study in which CBD may raise peak THC, whereas the results give only the authors' suggestion of a slight rise with wide variability (p. 17); the claim follows the results. Pulse: ten studies; the review's eight with no difference (seven names, Dalton standing for both experiments) plus Nicholson make nine of ten; Karniol both directions (pp. 19-20). Intoxication: two of nine reduced (Dalton smoked, n = 15; Zuardi oral, n = 8), seven not; the Dalton among the seven is the oral-pretreatment experiment (Table 1, p. 66), so seven of nine is consistent. Anxiety and psychosis-like effects, the four oral or intravenous studies, the 48-person vaporised crossover and the 14-person vaporised anxiety result all match pp. 21-23; no statistical test is given for Karniol's 4 of 5 against 3 of 15. Cognitive and psychomotor results go both ways (pp. 24-29). The review's route and dose summary (p. 15) disagrees with Table 1, as the magnitude says: I count oral THC in 5 studies (text 6), vaporised THC in 3 including Arkell at 13.75 mg (text 2 at 8 mg), CBD routes summing to 15 of 16, a 4 mg vaporised CBD dose no study used, 0.320 mg/kg (Bird, oral) listed as smoked CBD, and an oral THC range of 10-40 mg whose 40 mg is Hollister and Gillespie's CBD dose (their THC was 20 mg). Findings only: doses appear as study conditions; nothing in this part reads as advice.

anchors.locator: 2.2 Eligibility criteria, 2.2.1.1 Inclusion criteria (continues p. 10, with 2.2.2 Exclusion criteria)
anchors.extracted: Included: a condition or group given acute THC; a matched condition or group given the same THC dose together with CBD under experimental conditions; THC by the same route in both; a placebo condition or a no-drug control such as a pre-drug baseline; peer-reviewed; English. Excluded: no matched THC dose and route with and without CBD; repeated dosing; no direct statistical comparison of THC alone with THC plus CBD; non-human studies.

Search on 28 February 2019 (MEDLINE, EMBASE, PsycINFO, CINAHL Plus; English and human filters): 1808 records, 601 duplicates; four articles published after the search added; 1211 titles and abstracts screened; 47 full texts; 23 articles reporting 16 studies included.

anchors.locator: 3.1 Study characteristics, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (2nd continues p. 14)
anchors.extracted: 16 studies in 23 articles (list of 21 names, Karniol 1974 to Arkell 2019). All experimental human laboratory studies; three parallel-group (Bird 1980, Englund 2013, Karniol 1974), the rest crossover; sample sizes 4 to 155, 466 participants in total; two designed for safety and pharmacokinetics and not powered for treatment effects; one parallel and five crossover studies with fewer than 10 (4-8) per treatment cell.

All studies used healthy volunteers; all except two (Karniol 1974, Zuardi 1982) included only people with previous cannabis use. Considerable variability in THC and CBD doses, THC:CBD ratio and route. Route summary: CBD oral 8 studies (5.4-800 mg), intravenous 1 (5 mg), vaporised 2 (4-16 mg), smoked 2 (0.150-0.320 mg/kg), oromucosal 2 (10-15 mg); THC oral 6 (10-40 mg), intravenous 3 (1.25-2 mg), smoked 3 (42 mg or 0.215-0.025 mg/kg), vaporised 2 (8 mg), oromucosal 2 (10-15 mg). Five pre-treatment designs: oral CBD 200-1500 mg 480 to 90 min before, smoked 0.150 mg/kg 30 min before, or intravenous immediately before THC; these had no pure placebo condition and used baseline measures.

anchors.locator: Table 1, Participants, Intervention and Risk of Bias columns
anchors.extracted: Cannabis use: Arkell at most 2 times a week (14; three did not complete); Bhattacharyya mean lifetime 150 times (6); Bird 50% at least weekly, 1-13 years of use (161 recruited, 6 excluded); Dalton two experiments, 16 and 8 men, at least once but never regularly; Englund at least once, mean lifetime 119-137 times (48); Guy and Robson at least once (24); Haney current use (31); Hindocha/Morgan 24 daily and 24 recreational (48); Hollister and Gillespie at least once (15); Hunt 4-10 times (4); Karniol 22 at least once and 18 never (40); Freeman/Lawn at least 4 times in the last year and at most 3 times a week (17); Nadulski at least once, never regularly (28 recruited, 20-24 analysed); Nicholson at least once, never regularly (8); Zuardi at least once, 3 never (8). Pre-treatment: T-5 min intravenous (Bhattacharyya), T-30 min (Dalton), T-90 min (Haney), T-210 min (Englund), T-480, -300, -120 min (Hunt). Vaporised THC 13.75 mg (Arkell) and 8 mg (two UCL studies). Overall risk of bias: 10 low, 6 some concerns.

anchors.locator: 3.4 Risk of bias within studies; 3.5 Risk of bias across studies
anchors.extracted: Ten studies at low risk of bias (nine names; Dalton covers two experiments), six with some concerns (Bird, Hollister and Gillespie, Hunt, Karniol, Nadulski, Zuardi), none high. Publication bias judged low because many studies report a mix of significant and non-significant results; English-only restriction; two industry-funded studies (Guy and Robson; Nicholson); possible residual effects of participants' own cannabis use; placebo condition possibly identifiable.

anchors.locator: 3.6 Synthesis of results; 3.6.1 Pharmacokinetic effects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Narrative synthesis because heterogeneity of outcomes precluded meta-analysis. Pharmacokinetics assessed in eight studies; typically CBD did not significantly alter THC's pharmacokinetic profile; three studies suggested a small effect on metabolism, inconsistent. Arkell (n = 14): vaporised THC 13.75 mg with CBD 13.75 mg, significantly higher peak plasma THC than THC 13.75 mg alone; AUC 0-3 h higher, not significantly. Nadulski (n = 24): oral CBD 5.4 mg partly inhibited hydroxylation of oral THC 10 mg; the authors suggest a slight rise and earlier peak; wide variability.

anchors.locator: 3.6.1 Pharmacokinetic effects, 2nd to 4th paragraphs (4th continues p. 19)
anchors.extracted: Guy and Robson (n = 24): time to peak plasma THC significantly later after oromucosal THC 10 mg with CBD 10 mg than THC 10 mg alone; no other significant PK differences; wide variability. Hunt (n = 4): oral CBD at 8, 6 and 2 h before (total 1500 mg) intravenous THC 2 mg, no significant PK effect (clearance 17 against 20.9 ml/min/kg). Hollister and Gillespie (n = 15): more urinary THC metabolites with oral CBD 40 mg, attributed to CBD itself. Bhattacharyya (n = 6) and Englund (n = 36) no difference in THC levels; Nicholson no comparison reported (p. 19).

anchors.locator: 3.6.2.1 Pulse rate, 1st paragraph; 2nd paragraph on p. 20
anchors.extracted: Ten studies reported pulse (four with methodological concerns). Eight found THC alone and THC with CBD raised pulse against baseline or placebo with no significant difference between them (seven names listed: Bird, Dalton, Freeman 2018, Guy and Robson, Haney, Hollister and Gillespie, Zuardi). Nicholson (n = 8): no difference in pulse over 30 min. Karniol (n = 40, 5 per group, p. 20): oral THC 30 mg raised pulse; with oral CBD 15 mg it seemed to rise further, with 30 or 60 mg the rise was reduced.

anchors.locator: 3.6.3 Subjective intoxicating effects (begins p. 20); Table 1, Dalton rows (p. 66)
anchors.extracted: Of nine studies (mostly VAS), two small studies found CBD reduced intoxication: Dalton (double-blind crossover, n = 15) smoked THC 0.025 mg/kg with CBD 0.150 mg/kg reduced feeling high and CMI effects; Zuardi (n = 8) oral THC 0.5 mg/kg with CBD 1 mg/kg reduced the ARCI-Ma rise. Seven found no evidence (Arkell, Bird, Dalton, Freeman 2018, Haney, Hindocha 2015, Roser 2009). Table 1 shows two Dalton experiments: CBD smoked with THC reduced feeling high; oral CBD 30 min before smoked THC altered no measure.

Three studies, two with unclear risk of bias (Karniol, Zuardi). Karniol (placebo-controlled double-blind parallel, n = 40, 5 per group; graded 0-4 scale, grade 4 including panic): oral THC 30 mg gave grade 4 effects in 4 of 5; with oral CBD 15, 30 or 60 mg, 3 of 15; none in the highest CBD group; no statistical test given. Zuardi (double-blind crossover, n = 8): oral CBD 1 mg/kg attenuated the STAI rise after oral THC 0.5 mg/kg. Arkell (n = 14): vaporised THC 13.75 mg with and without CBD 13.75 mg gave small significant rises in anxiety ratings and STAI at 15 min; still raised after an hour only without CBD.

anchors.locator: 3.6.5 Psychotomimetic and psychosis-like experiences, 1st paragraph (continues p. 23) and 2nd paragraph (p. 23)
anchors.extracted: Three studies, no bias concerns. Bhattacharyya (double-blind, pseudo-randomised crossover): intravenous THC 1.25 mg gave psychosis-like PANSS effects in 3 of 6; intravenous CBD 5 mg beforehand, against placebo, ameliorated them. Englund (randomised double-blind parallel, n = 48): after intravenous THC 1.5 mg, no difference in the mean PANSS rise between oral CBD 600 mg and placebo pre-treatment; fewer given CBD had a clinically significant rise in positive symptoms (at least 3 points); SSPS paranoia lower with CBD. Morgan (double-blind placebo-controlled crossover, n = 48): vaporised THC 8 mg with or without CBD 16 mg did not differ; both raised BPRS negative symptoms and PSI scores.

anchors.locator: 3.6.6.1 Episodic memory and 3.6.6.2 Attention and working memory (begin p. 24)
anchors.extracted: THC alone impaired episodic memory in five studies. Englund: CBD pre-treatment left immediate-recall impairment unchanged but lessened delayed-recall impairment, and did not seem to change THC's impairment of working-memory tasks including digit span. Morgan: same impairment with or without CBD (prose recall, N-back). Karniol: time-production change after THC absent with CBD. Arkell (n = 14): DSST impaired 20 min after THC alone but not with CBD; divided attention more impaired with CBD than after THC alone or placebo.

Roser 2009 (n = 24): right-hand tapping reduced against placebo after oral THC 10 mg with CBD 5.4 mg, not after THC alone; THC alone impaired left-hand tapping in 2 of 5 sessions. Arkell (n = 14): lane weaving increased with THC 13.75 mg with and without CBD. Bird (parallel, 16 groups, n given as 116): oral CBD 0.320 mg/kg did not modify impairment by oral THC 0.215 mg/kg. Dalton (n = 16): smoked THC 0.025 mg/kg impaired steadiness, hand-eye coordination and dexterity with and without CBD 0.150 mg/kg.

23 papers, 16 studies, 466 participants. CBD may moderate some effects of THC, most commonly a reduction, but not consistently across studies; considerable heterogeneity of routes, doses and THC:CBD ratios; no consistent pattern across these factors, so a dose-response relation could not be determined; oral CBD doses 5.4-800 mg, with low oral bioavailability (13-19%, cited from another source).

anchors.locator: 4.1 Pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic effects, 1st paragraph (continues p. 33)
anchors.extracted: Two studies (Arkell; Nadulski) showed that CBD with THC may lead to increased peak plasma THC, one a delayed time to peak (Guy and Robson), four non-significant findings (Bhattacharyya, Englund, Hollister and Gillespie, Hunt); most studies small with no significant PK differences. Across studies THC with and without CBD generally increased pulse (p. 33).

anchors.locator: 4.2 Subjective intoxication; 4.3 Anxiety and psychosis-like experiences (continues p. 34)
anchors.extracted: Intoxication was predominantly experienced similarly with and without CBD. Three studies said to show that 'significantly fewer participants experienced extreme feelings of anxiety and psychotic-like effects' with CBD, although the results give no test for Karniol's counts and no difference in Englund's mean (pp. 21-23); the authors propose CBD may act only when THC's effects are extreme (Englund: clinically significant rises but not mean rises reduced, p. 34).

anchors.locator: 4.7 Strengths and limitations (end, begins p. 37); 4.8 Conclusions; declarations
anchors.extracted: Methodological issues: limited information on withdrawals, inadequate description of randomisation, allocation blinding and order effects; very small samples, some underpowered; multiplicity not always handled. Conclusion: some evidence CBD may reduce some effects of THC, with significant variability between studies and between people within studies. Declarations of interest: none; no specific grant.

p. 15 and Table 1 rows on pp. 68, 69 and 71 as stated.
p. 16 names nine; Table 1 rates both Dalton experiments low, giving ten low and six some concerns.

pp. 17-19 as stated. Not mentioned: Hollister and Gillespie's higher urinary metabolites with CBD (attributed to CBD itself) and Roser 2009's sex difference in metabolites (pp. 17-18); the discussion (pp. 32, 36) counts Nadulski as a second study in which CBD may raise peak THC, which the results do not show.
pp. 19-20, values match (10.3, 4.4 and 5.1 mmHg; n = 17 and 31; CBD 200, 400, 800 mg; THC about 42 mg).

pp. 20-21 and Table 1 (p. 66): my reading agrees that the Dalton among the seven is the oral-pretreatment experiment (8 men, no measure altered) and the reducing one is CBD smoked with THC (16 enrolled, one withdrew).
pp. 21-22, 3.6.4: all values match; no test is given for Karniol's counts.

pp. 22-23 and Table 1, p. 65, as stated. Not noted: the Bhattacharyya row gives the CBD pre-treatment as T-5 min in the Intervention column and T-210 min in Main findings, and the text says immediately before (p. 15).

'digit span was unchanged' can be read as digit span not being impaired. The review says CBD pre-treatment did not seem to alter THC's impairing effects on working-memory tasks, including digit span forward and backward (3.6.6.2, p. 25). Suggested wording: 'and CBD did not change THC's impairment of working memory, including digit span'.
pp. 28-29 as stated. Worth adding for balance: in Roser 2009, THC alone impaired left-hand tapping in 2 of 5 sessions, associated with higher 11-OH-THC (p. 29).

Text (p. 30): THC with CBD increased wakefulness and stage 3 sleep; THC alone increased sleepiness 30 min after waking. Table 1 (p. 71): THC with CBD, not THC alone, decreased stage 3 sleep and increased time awake; both increased sleepiness after waking. Disagreement confirmed.
Table 1, p. 65 (Arkell: one discharged for raised blood pressure and heart rate), p. 70 (three participants had a panic attack) and note d, p. 72 (three women); conditions not stated.
p. 31, 2nd paragraph (13-19% bioavailability, oral CBD 5.4-800 mg) and 4.8 Conclusions, p. 38.

reporting_issues.note: Table 1, p. 65: 'Vaporised THC 3.75 mg + CBD 13.75 mg'; THC-alone condition 'CBD < 1.25 mg'; the text gives 13.75 mg on pp. 17, 22, 25, 26 and 29.
p. 19 gives sublingual THC 10 mg with or without CBD 10 mg; p. 30 and Table 1 (p. 71) 15 mg oromucosal spray; stage 3 direction differs; Table 1 rates low risk with 'Randomisation not indicated'.
161 recruited with six excluded (p. 66), 166 divided into 16 groups (note a, p. 72), n = 116 (p. 29); 155 is the only figure consistent with the stated maximum and the total of 466.
Table 1 body: 26 placebo and 22 CBD (p. 67); note b: placebo 22 and CBD 26 (p. 72); n = 36 for plasma (p. 19).
Two Dalton rows in Table 1 (p. 66, continued p. 67); n = 15 on p. 21, 16 on pp. 26 and 29; pre-treatment smoked in the text (p. 15) but oral in Table 1 (p. 66).

My counts from Table 1 agree. One more mismatch: the text's oral THC range of 10-40 mg (p. 15) includes 40 mg, which in Table 1 is Hollister and Gillespie's CBD dose (their THC was 20 mg); the highest oral THC in mg is Karniol's 30 mg.
Wall et al. (2019) appears in the rows on p. 68 and p. 70; Hindocha et al. (2019) is not named in Table 1; the p. 13 list names 21 articles.

RoB2 named with Higgins et al. (2011) on p. 12; Higgins et al. (2016) on p. 37; 'unclear risk of bias' on p. 21 against 'Some concerns' in Table 1; Bhattacharyya pseudo-randomised but rated low (p. 65).
p. 30: 'By contrast, CC and A carriers did differ on attentional bias following THC+CBD', after a sentence describing a difference after THC alone; a missing negation is likely.

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2 without meta-analysis; critically low follows from items 4 and 13. Item 13 is a close call, as the card says, but the discussion draws its anxiety and psychosis conclusion as 'significantly fewer' from studies including two with some concerns while calling risk of bias typically low, so 'no' is defensible.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor overall because the abstract is hedged; the discussion's statement on anxiety and psychosis-like effects (p. 33) is the gap most likely to travel, and the card records it.

missed: Cannabis-use frequency: the card's 'mostly with occasional use' (cannot_establish) and 'most other samples had used occasionally' (sample demographics) are not established by Table 1: about half of Bird et al.'s 155 used at least weekly (p. 66), 24 of the 48 in the Hindocha/Morgan study used daily (p. 68), Haney et al.'s 31 were current users (p. 68), and Englund, Guy and Robson, Hollister and Gillespie and Karniol give only 'at least once' (pp. 67, 69). The claim's 'mostly occasionally' appears to come from here.
Men-only samples: counting Dalton's two experiments as Table 1 does, six studies enrolled men only (Dalton twice, Guy and Robson, Hollister and Gillespie, Hunt, Karniol), not five.
Hunt et al.'s CBD timing differs between the text (8, 6 and 2 h before THC, p. 18) and Table 1 (480, 300 and 120 min, p. 69).
Arkell et al.: Table 1 says three of the 14 did not complete (p. 65), while the text uses n = 14 throughout.
